To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the total and regional body composition measures were significantly related to CRP, 2) total and regional estimates were significantly related to each other, 3) total and regional measures were better predictors of CRP than BMI, and 4) the best predictors of CRP were the total estimates of fat and lean mass.
the use of body composition measures, such as BMI, skinfold thicknesses, and waist circumference, are poor indicators of inflammation in young Hispanic girls.
anthropometric measurements and body composition indices were not good predictors of inflammation in Hispanic girls.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development, implementation and evaluation of interventions designed to improve the health and well‐being of children and their families.
understanding the social and cultural factors which influence the health and well‐being of individuals.
the study of the human body in relation to the environment, and the development of new technologies to improve the quality of life.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
anthropometry and imaging techniques are equally valid in predicting inflammation among Hispanic girls, but that the prediction of inflammation using imaging is superior to that of anthropometry.
there is no evidence that a Mediterranean dietary pattern has a significant effect on C‐reactive Protein (CRP) levels in healthy individuals.
anthropometry, in particular BMI, and imaging, in particular MRI, are both valid and reliable for assessing body composition in young Hispanic children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
anthropometry is a better predictor of inflammation in young girls than are imaging‐based techniques.

the use of body mass index and body fat percentage as measures of adiposity in the prediction of inflammation is inadequate and that the measurement of body composition using dual‐energy X‐ray absorptiometry (DXA), computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more accurate.

the use of anthropometry and body fat percentage (BF%) is more accurate than the use of imaging techniques (dual energy x‐ray absorptiometry [DXA] and magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) for the prediction of CRP among Hispanic girls.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the body mass index (BMI), a common measure of adiposity, is not an accurate measure of body fat in children and adolescents.
the combination of imaging and anthropometry provides a better prediction of inflammation compared with imaging alone.
anthropometry is an effective and inexpensive way to assess body composition and its relationship to health.
